To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) brain activity during observation of and simulation of a dance sequence increases as dancers learn to dance that sequence outside the scanner; 2) activity in inferior parietal cortex and ventral premor cortex increases as dancers' ratings of the ease with which they can perform the observed movement increase; 3) these findings suggest that action simulation can be built de-novo over 5 weeks.
dancers who rehearsed a novel complex dance sequence for 5 weeks outside the scanner showed enhanced premotor and paraital activity when simulating the movement inside the scanner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of motor resonance, which is defined as a resonance of the observer's motor system in response to the observation of another person's action.
how the brain represents the motor actions of others and how this is modulated by the observer's own motor expertise and ability.
how we learn to simulate the actions of others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain areas engaged during imagined dance are modulated as a result of the amount of actual practice and that these changes are reflected in the dancers' ability to perform the movements.

the present study demonstrates that the brain regions classically involved in action simulation are sensitive to the ability to perform an action, and that these regions are active during the observation of a complex motor skill that is learnt and rehearsed de novo.
motor experience is a critical determinant of motor resonance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the motor resonance system can be trained de novo, and that the degree of activity in the system is modulated by the ability to perform the action.
the brain regions that are classically associated with action simulation and observation are also sensitive to the amount and quality of motor experience, even when the movement is novel.
the more you know how to perform a movement, the more you can imagine it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
action observation and action simulation are not the same.
the ability to simulate actions is not a unitary phenomenon, and the degree to which we can simulate an observed movement is dependent upon both the amount of practice and our own motor expertise.
the brain regions classically engaged during action observation and action simulation are sensitive to motor experience.
